The time falls at each doubling across the table, by under two percent from 48 to 96, since the matrix does not move and only the attempts do. Each attempt samples and commits the accumulator's digits, the merge's worth and the stages', so the fewer attempts of a wide mask are the whole gain within the measure. The transaction measure alone would therefore take the widest mask on its grid: every transaction-sized application's least is at the grid's top, 1,024, at every sampler rate (the device's statement alone, one compression, is left out, since its transaction is its merges). The minimum is shallow: the recovery circuit is within two percent of it from α = 54 up. What a wider mask costs is outside the measure: the coordinate width, 25 bits at 48 and 29 at 1,024, which sets the handed-over accumulator's size and the peak memory's mask; a tenth slice from 360, which the transfer and the aggregator's range checks pay; and the rate of the public merges, which does not move here. The page keeps 48, nine slices a coordinate and 1.3 attempts, within 9.1 percent of the measure's least for every transaction-sized application at the page's sampler and 25 at Karney's rate. Nine slices hold up to a width of 300, where the attempts are 1.04, so a wider mask within nine slices is open.

The transaction's shape

The fold is paid once per transaction, so a transaction with four recovery inputs takes 0.279 s per note at rank 22. What does not help: the two-matrix design of the note's §5.9, whose switch costs an in-circuit opening; the bimodal variant, which needs a structure that hides a sign (the note's open point 9); and masking in blocks (its §5.7), which is open.

BitZ

BitZ's zero-knowledge rows are derived, since its paper offers succinctness only. Ligero's random row per Ligerito level puts one symbol in every opened column, so that the columns reveal nothing. That is 16 bytes per opened column in the decider's proof under ARC, about 23 kbytes at 128 bits with the three first-round trees, and nothing under recursion. Each sum-check gets a Libra-style mask polynomial: Flock's zero-check and lincheck, Zinc+'s PIOP and each layer of the GKR, a sum of univariates of degree three in each variable. The masks are committed as extra rows of the same Ligerito matrix under those random rows and opened with the witness, so that each sum-check runs over the masked polynomial. The masks are 1,600 field elements for a 225-bit witness, under a percent of the step, paid in the fold. Zook-style spot-checked mask oracles would cost about 100 kbytes here, one oracle per sum-check round over the GKR's 325 rounds, so they are not the choice. Whether ARC's accumulation preserves zero knowledge is not examined for BitZ either.

Security floor

Akita's catalog sizes every matrix so that the cheapest known attack on its Module-SIS instance costs at least 128 bits under the ADPS16 quantum core-SVP model, 20.265β for BKZ block size β. That puts every instance at block size 484 to 486. ARC's openings are counted at the same λ, and the F2​ family's optimizer runs at the floor, which shrinks its lists.

The accumulation matrix that the lattice rows commit under is sized the same way. For each row the model takes the cheapest module rank and ring degree, among the catalog's 512 and 1,024, that Akita's ℓ∞ estimator certifies at the floor for the row's bound, with the row's accumulator as the width, from the estimator's own width tables at the catalog's bound ladder, the bound rounded up to the ladder. The bound is the one the zero-knowledge note's extraction argument needs: without the mask a fold's output, the two children at the challenge's weight and the step's own digits, and with the mask the response's width 14σ at the row's own accumulator, times the extraction's slack. The zero-knowledge section says what the mask adds; without it every row is at rank 1, as the catalog's own accumulation matrix is.

The 147‑bit floor, the page's default, re-plans Akita's catalog at that floor with Akita's own planner, so its openings are planned rather than scaled. It is 147 rather than 150 because Akita's rank-one compression maps certify at 147.3 bits at the catalog's geometry; the margin section below explains. The rank growth at that floor is applied to the inner images' share of the verification; the accumulation matrix that every step commits under is looked up in the floor's own table, as the margin section says. That share is the terminal's clear inner images at the shipped geometry, 1,344 coordinates whose bytes Module-SIS sets independently of the modulus. They are 33 percent of the opening at the 128-bit field, 35 on Goldilocks, 30 with 64-bit commitments, 26 with Pasta images at SIS size, and 42 with Pasta for everything, where they are 32-byte field elements. The verifier's work is taken to divide as the message does.

WHIR's proofs, measured over both fields, are 16 percent larger at 147 bits than at 128, and ARC's openings grow with the floor; the margin section below has both.

Pedersen-IPA over Pasta rests on the discrete logarithm in a group of order near 2254: about 126 classical bits by Pollard rho, and nothing against a quantum adversary. It is shown at the 128‑bit floor as the conventional pre‑quantum baseline, and under the arithmetic-hash option, since its circuits hash with Poseidon, so the page's defaults do not show it. It drops out at 147 bits, which it does not reach even classically.

The binary-groups row is shown at 128 bits only too, since its Module-SIS certificate is not yet issued.

The table's Assumption column names what each family rests on: the discrete logarithm on Pasta, Module-SIS with a random oracle, or a random oracle alone. It is one of the dominance test's requirements (Pasta and the scheme assumption). The next section says how much to trust the Module-SIS figures.

Grinding

The hash-based families can spend proof of work in the query phase: with g bits of grinding the queries need carry only λ−g bits. So ARC's openings per input fall to 2(λ−g)/log2​(1/ρ), and WHIR's own query counts fall in the same way. A fixed setting applies to every hash-based row at once, from none, 16, 20 and 24 bits. The default, best per row, gives each configuration the measured setting with the smallest prover, from a wider set of measurements, and the row's label says which.

Each row's proof size is measured at its setting with the reference implementation over both fields, rates 1/2 to 1/64, at 217, 218 and 220, with the growth per doubling taken over the three doublings. The earlier rows were measured at 20 bits while ARC's openings were counted without grinding, which this corrects. At rate 1/8 over the 256‑bit field the proof is 147 kbytes with no grinding, 130 kbytes at 16 bits, 126 kbytes at 20 and 121 kbytes at 24; at rate 1/32 it is 113 kbytes, 100 kbytes, 96 kbytes and 93 kbytes.

The prover pays 2g evaluations of the grinding hash per merge, taken as the family's own Merkle hash so that the merge circuit's check is one node per input. Each bit of grinding removes about one opening in a hundred, so about a percent of the circuits and of the prover, while the grinding's cost doubles. The prover is least where the two cross: at 17 to 19 bits for families with Poseidon trees (217 permutations are about 0.5 percent of a merge's prover at rate 1/8 and rank 13, 220 about 4 percent), and 12 to 18 bits for the F2​ family and BitZ. The minimum is shallow, within a percent from 16 to 20 bits.

With BLAKE3 trees, the default, the WHIR-type rows take 24 bits, the most measured, since 224 compressions are a small part of a merge spread over tens of thousands of circuits. The settings and the lower rates follow Ulrich Haböck's questions. The capacity regime, which would halve the openings again, is not offered, since its conjectures were refuted.

Hashes in circuits

Every hash that a merge circuit computes is one of two. The default is a conventional hash, BLAKE3, at 14,900 gates per 64-byte compression in a lookup-free R1CS over Pasta or Goldilocks and about 200 word multiplications natively. The option allows an arithmetic hash, Poseidon 1.1 over the circuit's own field: 288 gates per Pasta permutation absorbing four elements, about 480 for the width-12 Goldilocks one, and 35,000 or 7,200 word multiplications natively.

Arithmetic hashes deserve consideration on the merits: for large fields and the widths in question, none of the attacks on Poseidon 1.1 has come near an academic break, and Tachyon uses it. The reason to exclude them by default is future-proofing. For long-term storage that reason is decisive, though some of a proof system's hashes are ones that long-term storage does not depend on. If requiring conventional hashes causes only a small regression that does not affect deployability, they are the choice; the option shows what the arithmetic hash buys.

With the option the rows priced with Poseidon join the BLAKE3 ones rather than replace them. So a configuration that is better on some measure with the conventional hash stays on the plot, and each frontier takes the better of the two. Ragu's checked-in circuits use Poseidon 1.1, so the Pedersen-IPA rows exist only under the option.

What the default changes: Akita's merge absorbs its transcript, 4 to 9 kbytes, in 55 to 133 compressions instead of 146 to 218 Poseidon atoms. So the merge grows from about 25 thousand gates to 0.83 million at the 128‑bit field and on Goldilocks and 2.0 million for the Pasta variants, at rank 16. Each step circuit's evaluation claim then costs more to absorb than a rank-13 circuit holds, and a 32-byte claim more than a rank-14 circuit. So rank 13 has no Akita rows and rank 14 none for the Pasta variants, and the first ranks that hold them take 1,740 and 1,471 circuits.

At rank 16 the merge takes 51 circuits at the 128‑bit field and on Goldilocks and 122 for the Pasta variants, against 2 with Poseidon. So the merge prover is 26 times the Poseidon one at the 128‑bit field (6.3e9 against 2.5e8) and 28 times on Goldilocks (6.6e8 against 2.4e7), whose wider BLAKE3 accumulator at the 64‑bit modulus takes the matrix to degree 1,024 at this floor; 61 times for the Pasta variants, and 67 with 64‑bit commitments, for the same reason. The proof grows by 4 to 4 kbytes at the small fields and by 10 to 11 kbytes with Pasta claims, from the per-circuit claims, and the atoms by 49 to 120. The per-step commitment cost and the decider are unchanged. The lever that would recover most of this is to aggregate the step circuits' claims before absorption, a design change.

For the WHIR-type rows every Merkle node becomes a BLAKE3 compression, so the merge grows 35 to 61 times (1.3 to 76 million gates for WHIR over Pasta at rate 1/8 and rank 13, 614 to 37,225 circuits). The prover grows 1.3 to 2.0 times for WHIR over either field and for FRI, since the trees get cheap but the circuits multiply. The limb hybrid's prover instead falls 2.2 times, since its Poseidon over limbs is dear natively. The decider's verification falls 17 to 83 times, to a few milliseconds; the proofs grow by a sixth with the larger batched witness, and the best grinding moves to 24 bits.

The F2​ family, BitZ and the binary-groups family hash with BLAKE3 already and do not change, so under the default their comparison with Akita is like for like. At rate 1/8 the F2​ family's ARC row proves a merge in 5.8e8 word multiplications for a proof of 214 kbytes, against Akita over Goldilocks at rank 16 with 6.6e8 and 77 kbytes. Its merge is 19 to 91 million AND gates against Akita's 0.83 million Pasta gates, which are not the same unit.

Transaction prover

The transaction prover measure prices a whole transaction rather than one merge, so that the cost of zero knowledge can be seen against the steps it belongs to. The transaction proves an application chosen above: the Ironwood recovery circuit; a transaction with four recovery inputs, which is four of the circuit under one zero-knowledge handoff; or a number of Merkle path checks of 32 levels and the leaf; or the hardware wallet's part of the recovery statement on its own, or a Zoodles transaction of two inputs and two outputs, both priced in the application subsection; the Tachyon transactions have the next section.

The application is costed component by component in each family's own arithmetization, under the selected hash policy. The family's steps are then as many as hold it, rounded up, since a transaction smaller than a step pays a whole step. A step circuit of rank r commits 2r coefficients, which is 2r−2 gates of four wires for the field arithmetizations, 2r bits or digits for BitZ and Kishu, and 222 AND gates for the Boolean families, which have no rank. Each step is committed at the family's per-step cost, which is the row's prover divided by its circuits, and there are as many merges at the row's accumulation prover, the merge's commitments and the fold's sum-checks.

The application in each arithmetization

Off Pasta the recovery circuit's curve arithmetic is emulated, in the ways the requirements section lists: about 14,500 multiplications in Pallas's base field, in five fixed-base and one variable-base scalar multiplication with complete additions, 160 Sinsemilla chunk additions and the nullifier's Poseidon. Its seven BLAKE2b compressions, the chunks' generator selections and its Merkle path are bit operations and cost about the same gates in any prime field. Over Pasta the circuit is 570,000 gates with a Poseidon path and 1.05 million with a BLAKE3 one. Over Goldilocks a multiplication is about 1,100 gates, with nine 29‑bit limbs and no lookups, so the circuit is 16.5 and 17.0 million gates; at a 128‑bit field, with 61‑bit limbs, about 700 gates give 10.7 and 11.2 million.

In a Boolean circuit a multiplication is about 120,000 AND gates, the 255‑bit product by Karatsuba and Toom–Cook and a Montgomery reduction by a prime of no special form. A 64‑bit addition is 64 ANDs and an XOR is free, so the hashes cost half their Pasta gates. The circuit is 1.73 billion AND gates, the multiplications nearly all of it.

In BitZ's integer arithmetization a multiplication is 510 committed bits, the value and the quotient, checked as one integer relation, while a hash gate is one bit and a 64‑bit addition 65, so the circuit is 8.4 million bits. In Kishu over Akita the claims are in one fixed field, so a multiplication is either 1,088 digits by the limb route or 510 by the fingerprint route, which pays per step instead. The circuit is 17 million or 8.5 million digits, plus its constraint PIOP, which the Kishu section prices. The bit arithmetizations hash the path with BLAKE3 under either policy, since Poseidon over Pallas's field would cost them 240 multiplications a node.

A Merkle path check is 33 nodes: 9,500 Pasta gates, or 15,600 Goldilocks or 128‑bit-field gates, with Poseidon in the field; 492,000 gates in any prime field with BLAKE3; 240,000 AND gates; or 497,000 bits or digits. So the recovery circuit's hashes are what make the bit arithmetizations cheap, a path-heavy application makes them cheaper still, and the Boolean families pay for every Pallas multiplication.

Two more applications price the hardware wallet's part of the Recovery Statement, which ZIP 2005's Option A proves on the device that holds the quantum spending key, the host proving the rest ([ZIP-2005], Key storage options). The device's own statement, qk=Hqk(qsk) with the linking commitment left out, is one BLAKE3 compression: 14,900 gates in any prime field, 7,170 AND gates, or 15,100 bits or digits. If the device instead signs SigHash with leanSPHINCS, the stateless hash-based signature of post-quantum Ethereum [EIP-8288] [Lit26], the host proves the verifier with the signature and the public key as witnesses. For [Wam26]'s pruned key that is 262 Keccak-f permutations or 298 BLAKE2s compressions, plus the 4,276-byte signature as input bits. XOR is not free in a digit arithmetization, so a Keccak-f permutation is 154,000 committed bits where a BLAKE2s compression is 21,300. What the wallet proves, what it hands over, and what the two routes cost on the device and in the transaction are the subject of the hardware-wallets chapter.

Zoodles is a sketch of a spend protocol with no curve arithmetic at all, named for the pasta-free noodle, and priced as a transaction of two inputs and two outputs. It keeps Tachyon's architecture (the next section): the same tree of spend, output, merge, and fee steps, and a note's membership and unspentness attested by a background lineage over the chain's anchors rather than by a Merkle path in the spend. The published tachygrams are roots of set polynomials that the merges multiply at the challenge: a spend's two epoch nullifiers, an output's commitment and padding, and the fee step's change commitment. In Tachyon the set polynomials are Pedersen vector commitments and the bridge hash is a Pedersen hash onto Pallas. Here they are the proof system's own committed vectors with evaluation claims, and the bridge hash is a BLAKE3 hash of the commitment, computed natively. A root then costs one multiplication in a 256-bit extension of the claim field, and an opening one more claim, absorbed by the merge above and folded by a few multiplications: 4,410 Kishu digits. The curve goes. Amounts are range-checked and summed in the PCD headers in place of value commitments and the binding signature. Spend authorization is chosen per input, usually the same for all: a Sprout-like preimage check, the payment key being the BLAKE3 hash of the authorizing key, which Tachyon's spend step derives already; or a leanSPHINCS signature with BLAKE2s at the pruned key over a transaction digest, verified in the circuit with the public key as a witness, since the zero-knowledge fold hides the key and no re-randomized signature is needed. The preimage check needs no digest: it is proved inside the spend step, which the tree binds to the rest of the transaction, directly and through the PCD headers. A signature is made outside the proof, so its message must bind the transaction's effecting data: each spend's two nullifiers, each output's commitment, the change commitment, the fee, and the epoch, 235 bytes or 4 compressions. The digest is a PCD header value: each spend verifies its signature over it, and the fee step recomputes it from the nullifiers and commitments that its children's headers carry, which a small transaction's headers hold. At the rank the signature transaction favours that hashing is under a tenth of one step; the signature verification is the expensive part. The fee step fixes the fee last and hashes the change note, the maximum-fee note's value less the fee, as Tachyon's does. Every hash is BLAKE3. The tree's 12 nodes hash 16 compressions in all, with 12 roots and 15 openings. The lineage's steps run in the background and are not in the transaction, as Tachyon's are not; one epoch of them is priced below.

In Kishu the preimage transaction is 313,000 digits and the signature one 13.1 million, the two verifiers being most of it. With zero knowledge Kishu proves the preimage transaction in 0.0824 s on one core at rank 19 and the signature one in 0.488 s at rank 21, so the preimage route is under a quarter of the signature route; without zero knowledge they are 0.0395 and 0.357 s. In the other families, preimage then signature: BitZ with zero knowledge 0.0837 and 0.263 s; Boolean over Akita 0.0767 and 0.153 s at its 128‑bit floor; Flock 0.195 and 0.389 s; and Akita over Goldilocks with a Poseidon tree 0.255 and 12.7 s. Tachyon's own four tachyactions, with their curve arithmetic, take 0.241 s in Kishu with zero knowledge and 0.168 without, and 0.298 s in BitZ, so Zoodles by preimage costs less in each, 34 percent of Tachyon with zero knowledge. A simpler Zoodles that proves a 32-level Merkle path in each spend, opening the note there and deriving one nullifier, with no set polynomials, is 1.21 million digits by preimage and 0.110 s with zero knowledge, 46 percent of Tachyon, and still costs less than Tachyon in Kishu and BitZ; by leanSPHINCS it is 0.491 s. Its two paths are most of its digits. The Pasta-native families reverse the order: with Pedersen-IPA under the arithmetic-hash option Tachyon is 8.44 s and the Merkle variant 44.3, since a path's hashes cost a prime field more than the curve does. Flock takes 10.5 s on Tachyon, 54 times its Zoodles figure, due to the Pallas multiplications in a Boolean circuit.

The lineage's own cost is the wallet's witness update, one step per note per epoch of 4,096 blocks, about 3.6 days at 75-second blocks: the shape of Tachyon's unspent lift. The step proves that the note's nullifier for the epoch is not among the epoch's published tachygrams. Tachyon attests that with a bucket, one residue profile's share of the epoch's tachygrams. The share is partitioned by whether x+Rj​ is a square at successive discriminants, down to at most 8,192 members (the size of its online polynomial slot), and folded as a set polynomial that the step opens at the nullifier. Over Pedersen a commitment folds in one scalar multiplication. Over digits the bucket's tachygrams would enter the wallet's accumulator element by element, 2.10 million bits or digits, and set its rank. Set polynomials are the right tool over Pedersen and a dear one over digits, so Zoodles uses a sorted Merkle tree instead. The builder sorts the epoch's tachygrams once for everyone and hashes consecutive pairs into the leaves, so an exclusion proof is one leaf, the nullifier's two neighbours, with its path. The step derives the epoch's nullifier, hashes the leaf, proves the path, compares the nullifier with both neighbours, and range-checks the epoch. For a tree of 1,048,576 tachygrams that is 22 hashes, 332,000 Kishu digits, under a sixth of the bucket's. The tree's size is a choice, 256 tachygrams a block over the epoch, between the bucket's 213 and a busy chain's 224. Each doubling adds one hash to the step, and a shorter epoch adds steps a day. Kishu takes 0.0395 s a note an epoch on one core at rank 19, without zero knowledge, since the lineage never leaves the wallet. BitZ takes 0.0832 s, Flock 0.195 s, Akita over Goldilocks 0.0319 s, and Pedersen-IPA 6.33 s at its 128‑bit floor. The lineage's best rank is the spend's own, so the spend that consumes it inherits a rank it would choose anyway: Zoodles by preimage at rank 19 is 0.0824 s with zero knowledge.

The masking fold

For Akita's zero-knowledge rows the user's masking fold is added. It is the expected rejection-sampling attempts, 1.3 at the page's Gaussian width, plus the handoff's merge. That merge is the small one that the note's §5.8 deferral leaves the user. It derives the challenge from the mask's commitments and its evaluations at the claims' points, checks the commitment identity on those images, and folds the claims, in whole step circuits of the rank. The decomposition of the response and the range and norm proofs are the aggregator's first fold's, which the zero-knowledge-layer merge that the accumulation prover prices already carries. Each attempt is a commitment of a mask the size of the accumulator under the masked accumulation matrix, and as many Gaussian samples at about 7.1 nanoseconds a sample as a rounded Gaussian with exact rounding, 21 word multiplications at the page's rate. The sampling does not depend on the modulus. The fold is paid once per transaction whatever it proves. The mask covers the user chain's last accumulator, the merge's circuits × 2rank digits and the stages'. The device's statement is the exception: the wallet hands over a bare leaf without a fuse of its own, so its mask covers the leaf's 2rank digits alone, and the merge that folds the leaf is the host's. The hash-based zero-knowledge rows likewise put their masked prover's extra work in the fold, once per transaction; under recursion that is their only zero-knowledge cost, since the public merges and the decider's proof are of public data. Pedersen-IPA's blinding is free. This is total work, not latency: the zero-knowledge note's §5.8 precomputes candidate masks in idle time and defers the decomposition to the aggregator, which leaves the device a sparse ring product and the transfer of the masked witness. An Orchard-style action has the recovery circuit's mix, with one path check and no BLAKE2b.

Results

For the recovery circuit, per note on one core, Kishu takes 0.283 s at rank 21, in 5 merges by the fingerprint route, and BitZ with ARC 0.262 s at rank 24, where one step holds the circuit; Akita with Pasta claims over 64‑bit commitments takes about 25.1 s at rank 17 with Poseidon, nearly all of it the fold's sum-checks over the accumulator's 85 digits per coefficient in Pasta's field, and 1,920 s at rank 17 under the default BLAKE3 trees; Akita over Goldilocks 16.1 s with Poseidon; and Pedersen-IPA, at its 128‑bit floor and the checked-in configuration, about 6.76 minutes, in 278 steps of rank 13, or 1.90 minutes at rank 17 with 72 endoscalings per step.

With zero knowledge Kishu's best is 0.370 s at rank 21 by the fingerprint route, and Akita with Pasta claims about 25.7 s at rank 17. BitZ stays at 0.263 s, having no rejection-sampling fold, with 23 kbytes more proof.

Tachyon transactions

The transaction options of 2, 4, 8 or 16 tachyactions, half spends and half outputs, keep Tachyon's own proof tree (tachyon-zcash/tachyon 73031f7, Stamp::prove). A spend is two steps, an output a seed and a step, each action after the first a merge, then the fee step and Ragu's rerandomization: 3s + 3o + 2 nodes for s spends and o outputs. The rerandomization is two fuses in Ragu as it is, each with the public bootstrap proof as the right child; Tachyon's pinned Ragu did it in one.

The page re-packs that tree for each rank's step size: a node larger than a step takes whole steps and its remainder joins the rest, which fill steps first-fit decreasing, and each rerandomization fuse is its own step. So at rank 13 over Pasta no two action circuits share a step and the merge rides with the fee step, 7 steps for two tachyactions against Tachyon's 8. At rank 15 every circuit of two tachyactions fits one step beside the two rerandomization fuses.

The nodes' circuits were measured through Ragu's synthesis analysis on Tachyon's steps at its header size of 9: 1,630 and 1,649 gates for a spend's two steps, 1,467 and 1,351 for an output's, 17 for an action merge and 1,934 for the fee step, in Pasta gates with Poseidon, all within rank 13's 2,048. In the other arithmetizations the transaction is Tachyon's circuits as they are, a pre-quantum protocol proven in a post-quantum proof system: the Poseidon permutations, 192 gates each in Ragu's gate model, are hashed under the page's policy; the fixed-base multiplications' window selections cost the bits' four monomials; and the window additions and the openings of staged values at ζ are Pallas multiplications. The remaining gates are the scalars' bit checks, the canonicity and range comparisons and the step's glue, priced as bit operations, one gate or committed bit each, which understates any among them that multiply field elements. So a node that is one step over Pasta is 6 to 8 steps of rank 17 over Goldilocks with Poseidon and 5 to 7 Boolean steps, which is where the range of step counts comes from. Pricing the remaining gates as multiplications too would give 27 to 39 Goldilocks steps.

Per-note steps that run in the background are not counted; a Zoodles note's lineage step, their counterpart, is an application of its own. A Tachyon transaction also needs Tachyon's header of nine elements, so while one is selected every row is shown at that header. The recovery circuit's options do the same, since its primary input needs six or seven elements.

On one core at the default floor, Pedersen-IPA at its own 128‑bit floor, two tachyactions take: with Pedersen-IPA at the checked-in configuration 7 fuses, 10.2 s, where Tachyon's own tree of 8 fuses is 11.7 s, and at rank 15 with 16 endoscalings per step 3 fuses, 6.33 s; Akita with Pasta claims over 64‑bit commitments 3.08 s at rank 15 with Poseidon; BitZ 0.265 s at rank 20; Kishu 0.144 s at rank 20 with Poseidon by the fingerprint route; Akita over Goldilocks 1.15 s in 36 steps with Poseidon; and the F2​ family 6.03 s in 31. With zero knowledge Akita with Pasta claims takes 4.33 s and Kishu 0.204 s, and BitZ is unchanged.

Sixteen tachyactions take: Pedersen-IPA 51.1 s in 35 steps at rank 13, or 19.0 s in 9 steps at rank 15; Akita with Pasta claims 5.58 s; BitZ 0.485 s; Kishu 0.283 s; Goldilocks 7.17 s.

For scale, Orchard's Halo 2 prover, measured on the same machine with assembly, takes 1.88 s for two actions and about 14 s for sixteen on one thread. So Tachyon on Pedersen-IPA is 3.6 to 5.4 times Orchard per action on one core, and about three times that again on all cores in the current implementation, which has had less attention to parallelization of the fuse.

How much to trust the Module-SIS parameters

Akita's advantage over the hash-based route rests on Module-SIS, where that route rests on a random oracle alone and Pedersen-IPA on the discrete logarithm. This section states what the parameters assume and where the uncertainty sits.

The sizing rule

Every matrix in Akita's catalog is sized so that the cheapest known attack on its Module-SIS instance costs at least 2128 operations under the quantum core-SVP model of [ADPS16]. That model charges 20.265β for lattice reduction with BKZ block size β and ignores the polynomial factors.

The block size that reaches a given root Hermite factor is taken from the BKZ 2.0 analysis of [CN11]. Every instance in the catalog lands at block size 484 to 486, in lattices of dimension 2,000 to 4,800. The catalog's own security check reports 128.26 bits on each.

A cross-check with the maintained lattice estimator [LE] agrees on the ranks. The estimator is maintained; the paper that introduced it, [APS15], is not, and its authors say so in a 2019 note. The estimator costs BKZ as 8n calls to an SVP oracle of the block size, with sieving per [BDGL16] classically and per [LMvdP15] and [Laa16] quantumly. It follows [ADPS16] for the primal attack, as [AGVW17] established, and leaves out the dimensions for free of [Duc18] and [ADH+19]. The same block size under other models:

Cost modelBits at β = 484, the 128‑bit floorAt β = 556, the 147‑bit floorSource
classical sieving, 20.292β141162[BDGL16]
quantum sieving, 20.265β, the floors used128147[Laa16], as adopted in [ADPS16]
"paranoid" lower bound, 20.2075β100115[ADPS16]

For calibration, ML-DSA [FIPS204], the standardized Dilithium, sizes its SIS instances at block sizes of about 423, 638 and 909 for its three security levels [Dil21]. These parameters therefore sit between its levels 2 and 3 on the same model.

Where the uncertainty sits

Three places, in decreasing order of concern.

  • Proof-level slack, not the assumption. Lattice schemes have slipped before by sizing for honest norms rather than the extractor's. Akita sizes for the extractor's collision bound, which is why the masked variant needs rank 340 against 143. But the knowledge-soundness proof in the quantum random-oracle model is still in progress. And the decoupled commitment modulus has no soundness argument yet beyond the LaBinius analogue. A gap of that kind moves parameters by a lot, not by twenty bits.
  • The instantiation is unusual. Ring dimension 64 with 128‑bit or 255‑bit moduli, compression rings of dimension 8 and 4, and norm bounds up to 248 are far from the regime of the standardized schemes. No attack exploits module structure beyond constant factors. Module-SIS has a worst-case reduction [LS15], and the quantum attacks on ideal lattices [CDW17] need principal ideals, which modules of rank 64 and more do not present. But there is less cryptanalytic attention on this corner, and the ℓ∞​ bounds take their own estimator route.
  • The cost model. Core-SVP is already a lower-bound style model. Refinements since 2016, such as the dimensions for free of [Duc18], have moved concrete estimates by ten to twenty bits either way. The disputed dual-attack improvements of [MATZOV22], reassessed in [DP23], concern LWE rather than SIS, which is attacked through the primal route. A 147‑bit quantum floor is 162 classical bits, and the paranoid model still gives 115; at 128 bits, 141 and 100.

Against the other assumptions

The hash-based route's assumption is weaker in the good sense: a random oracle and collision resistance only. Its soundness risk is concentrated in the proximity-gap conjectures, which is exactly where the 2025 refutations landed. The proven Johnson regime is therefore where that route is priced here.

Pedersen-IPA rests on the discrete logarithm on Pasta, about 126 classical bits and nothing against a quantum adversary. So the fair statement is that Akita dominates on efficiency while adding one assumption whose concrete hardness is estimated rather than proven. That assumption has SIS studied since [Ajt96], Module-SIS since [LS15], and standardization behind it.

A margin

The 147‑bit floor, the page's default, puts the block size at 556 against the 128‑bit floor's 484 to 486. The security-floor option above re-plans Akita's catalog at the higher floor with Akita's own planner. Its single security policy is retargeted to 147 bits, its runtime width tables are regenerated by its estimator at that floor, and its six rank-one compression cells are re-sized from them. So the openings at 147 bits are planned, not scaled.

The floor is 147 rather than 150 because the compression chain is built from rank-one maps. At the catalog's geometry its first map, at ring dimension 16 and width 4,096, certifies at 147.3 bits. A 150-bit floor allows that map a width of 3,806, so the chain would need rank-two maps, or two maps where it has one, and either doubles the compressed images at every level.

The accumulation matrix agrees about where the floor's cost begins. Of the 186 lattice rows shown at both floors, 10 take a larger matrix at 147 bits than at 128, every one a BLAKE3 row, whose merges' many circuits make the widest accumulators; Kishu's rows keep their matrices at 128, 147, and 150. At 150 bits 2 more would move, the unmasked matrix of the Pasta-claims rows with 64‑bit commitments, from degree 512 to 1,024.

The planner does not give the prover's rows term or the verifier's inner-image share. For those the model takes the weakest Module-SIS instance of each of the 115 schedules in the shipped catalog's security report and, for each, the smallest module rank that covers the instance's width at both floors. With the catalog's own mix of moduli the ranks sum to 121 at 128 bits and to 150 at 147 bits, a factor of 1.24, with 29 instances moving up a rank. Over a 64‑bit modulus, where the ranks are higher to begin with, the sums are 185 and 211, a factor of 1.14, with 26 moving. Over Pallas the instances sit at the width cap at both floors but one: the sums are 117 and 118, a factor of 1.01, with 1 moving.

Where the floor binds, the maximum secure widths shrink several-fold. At 147 bits the median shrink, over the cells where neither width is at the estimator's search cap and the width falls, is a factor of 2 to 3 at ring dimensions up to 32, 4 to 10 at 64, 4 to 13 at 128 and 256, and 6 to 15 at 512 and above, with the 32-bit modulus at the low end of each range. The few cells at the largest dimensions whose 147-bit width is still finite shrink about 36-fold.

The hash-based rows at the higher floor

The floor moves the hash-based rows too, through λ alone and independently of any lattice instance. WHIR's proofs, measured with the reference implementation at 217 over both fields at rates 1/2 to 1/8, are 16 percent larger at 147 bits than at 128, and its verifier's hashes 12 percent more; ARC's openings per input, 2(λ−g)/log2​(1/ρ), grow by 15 percent.

Akita proof sizes at a Pasta modulus: what can be computed now, and how

Written 2026-10-13. Companion to Zero knowledge for a lattice accumulation step. The question: what would an Akita opening proof cost if the base field were the Pallas base field (255 bits), as Tachyon and the Ironwood recovery circuit want, and what about Goldilocks. Akita’s planner cannot plan a schedule for a modulus that it does not know, so this note does two things. It re-prices every shipped schedule at the other field’s widths with Akita’s own byte formula. And it generates the SIS width tables that a real Pasta profile would need. The remaining work for a real profile is listed at the end.

1. What was built

All code lives in the scratch clone of LayerZero-Labs/akita at commit 60b82bc30f4f8f1130ccd71fe10b0b9bed909ab9 (2026-10-09, Apache-2.0 or MIT), under work/akita-src. The diff is small and self-contained:

  • akita-sis-estimator: two estimator-only moduli, pallas (the Pallas base field) and goldilocks (264−232+1), selectable in every example by name. They do not have any params profile, so the table generators emit CSV for them and the ℓ∞​ generator gives them the canonical role cells of the checked-in profiles as explicit origins. A small example, pasta_rank, binary-searches the least row count for a Euclidean bound at each modulus.
  • akita-params: NonterminalLevelLayout::with_field_widths, which re-prices a level’s atoms at other base-field and challenge-field widths without changing their counts.
  • akita-schedules: expanded_schedule_proof_breakdown, which splits a schedule’s proof estimate into non-terminal payloads, offloaded setup sum-checks, the terminal extension-opening reduction, the terminal response, and grinding nonces, at the schedule’s own widths or at a FieldWidthOverride. With no override its total equals the planner’s own estimate, and the example checks that on every row.
  • akita-schedules and akita-planner: a process-wide pricing width override, set_pricing_width_override, consulted by every byte estimate that the planner derives from a policy, and read by the artifact generator from AKITA_PRICING_WIDTHS. With it set, the planner selects schedules by their cost at the override widths (§3.1).
  • akita-planner: the example catalog_reprice, which loads every shipped schedule artifact, or those in a directory given by --artifacts, and prints the breakdown three times. Once at the schedule’s own modulus, once at Pallas widths (255-bit base and challenge field, no extension), and once at Goldilocks widths (64-bit base field, degree-2 challenge extension, as the fp64 presets use).
  • work/akita-pasta-estimates.sh: builds, runs the re-pricing and the rank ladder, then generates the full Euclidean and ℓ∞​ width tables for both new moduli as CSV. Outputs land in work/akita-pasta-out, one log per step and a summary with timings.

Reproduce the re-pricing alone with:

cd work/akita-src
RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.96.0 cargo run --release -p akita-planner --features catalog-gen --example catalog_reprice

2. What re-pricing means

The planner’s proof estimate is a byte formula over a schedule’s geometry (crates/akita-params/src/proof_size.rs and crates/akita-schedules/src/runtime.rs). Per non-terminal level it sums opening payloads and compressed images in base-field atoms, the range-tree, norm, and fused sum-checks in challenge-field atoms, and the next level’s compressed payload. The terminal adds the clear partials in base-field atoms and the digit-valued folded response at a variable width, and grinding nonces are priced separately.

Re-pricing keeps everything about the schedule fixed: fold levels, witness lengths, digit bases, sum-check shapes, terminal shape, nonces. It changes only the width of a base-field atom and of a challenge-field atom, and the claim extension degree used for the extension-opening reduction. So it prices “this schedule, serialized over that field”. It is not the schedule that the planner would choose for that field. Two effects go the other way:

  • Pallas has 85 base-8 digits per coefficient against 43 for the 128-bit field, so a natively planned Pasta witness is longer at every level, which adds sum-check rounds and possibly a level. This pushes the real figure up.
  • The planner would re-optimize levels, block counts, and the terminal shape for 32-byte atoms. This can push it down, and §3.1 measures it: about 6%.

The first effect cannot be quantified without a Pasta profile, which is the remaining work of §6. The re-pricing is the part of the answer that follows from the byte formula alone.

3. Results

The fp128 presets do not use any challenge extension and have a claim extension degree of one, so their geometry is the right template for a Pasta field, which would also use none. The fp32 and fp64 presets carry extension-opening partials that a Pasta schedule would not have, so their Pallas columns overstate and are not quoted here.
