The page’s choice, and §5.3’s, is α=48 with the weight-20 challenges. A narrower mask saves rank. α=12 takes the factor from 2.45 to 2.22 for 2.7 attempts instead of 1.3; α=6 brings 2.11 and a masked accumulator of 12.6 Mbytes for 7.5 attempts at about 0.26 s each; and α=4 buys little more for three times the attempts. A wider one saves attempts, which cannot fall below one while the rank keeps growing, and from α=59 the coordinates take a tenth slice. The page’s transaction measure prices the user’s whole chain, and in it each attempt commits the whole mask. On the page’s ℓ∞​ route (§5.5) the matrix does not move across these widths, so that measure alone prefers the widest mask, and 48 is within 9.1 percent of its least (its zero-knowledge section); what a wider mask costs there is outside the measure, the coordinates’ bits and slices in the transfer and the aggregator’s range checks, and the public merges’ rate. On this section’s Euclidean route a wider mask costs rank as well, which is the trade-off the table shows. These figures move the prover’s commitment work and the zero-knowledge layer’s accumulator, not the final proof, which §5.2 leaves nearly unchanged. The N​ in ∥z∥2​ is the larger term, and §5.7 considers masking in blocks to reduce it.

5.7 Masking in blocks

The N​ in ∥z∥2​ is the price of masking the whole vector at one width (§2.4). Masking block by block, zb​=yb​+cb​sb​ over B blocks of Nb​=N/B digits, replaces N​ by Nb​​: at B=256 that is four bits off the bound, a rank factor of 2.00 instead of 2.45 with §5.3’s parameters, or 1.70 instead of 2.11 at α=6, and 23-bit coordinates, eight digits, an accumulator of 12.6 Mbytes. The difficulty is making the rejection test independent per block. A rejected block resamples its mask, which changes the mask’s commitment and so the challenge; with one challenge for every block, one rejection restarts them all, and the acceptance probability M−B vanishes. Two ways around it:

  • Per-block challenges. A challenge cb​ per block, derived from Cyb​​, lets each block retry alone. But the fold identity Azb​=Ayb​+cb​Asb​ needs the block’s own inner image Asb​, and the accumulator’s commitment binds only the outer commitment of the concatenated images, ∑b​Bb​tb​ (Akita §4.5). With distinct cb​ the verifier cannot form ∑b​cb​Bb​tb​ from the one outer commitment. So the accumulator would carry B commitments per committed vector instead of one: compressed, 128 bytes each, 32 kbytes per vector at B=256, six vectors per step, and the merge absorbs them all, about 12,000 atoms against 180. The claims split the same way, into per-block partials, B per claim point, which Akita’s terminal already uses. At B=16 the saving is two bits and one digit, and the cost 16 commitments per vector and about 700 more atoms in the zero-knowledge layer’s merge. Not attractive.
  • One challenge, candidate masks. Keep one c, but sample k candidate masks per block before the challenge, bind all of them, derive c, and take for each block the first candidate that passes the rejection test against csb​, publishing the index. The index leaks nothing: the theorem of §2.2 makes the accepted output and the acceptance probability independent of the secret, so the index is geometric with parameter 1/M whatever s is. The probability that some block exhausts its k candidates is about B(1−1/M)k; at B=256 and M=1.3, k= 9 leaves 2−10. The cost is k times the mask sampling and the binding of kB candidate masks before the challenge. Akita’s compression maps are linear, so the binding can be a Merkle tree over the candidates’ compressed images, with the B chosen leaves opened in the merge circuit and summed: 256 paths of about 14 hashes, a million gates, plus 256 images of 128 bytes absorbed, about a thousand atoms, in the zero-knowledge layer’s merge only. A single lattice commitment to all candidates with the selection proven as a linear relation would be cheaper and is a further design. The masks’ commitments are the same Ay as before, so the extraction argument and the bound are unchanged apart from Nb​​.

The second route is the one worth pursuing, if the candidate binding can be made cheap; it is open. Either way these figures move the prover’s commitment work and the zero-knowledge layer’s accumulator and merge, not the final proof.

5.8 The user’s online cost

The fold of §3 runs once per transaction on the user's device: the 0.335 s of §5.4 on a fast core, a few seconds on a phone, which is still worth moving off the critical path. Two changes move nearly all of it.
  • Precomputed candidate masks. The masks depend on neither the witness nor the transaction, so the device samples a batch of k masks y1​,…,yk​ and commits to them, Cy,i​=Ayi​, in idle time. At transaction time the batch is bound into the transcript, the challenge c is derived, and the first candidate that passes the rejection test against cs is used, with its index published: the second route of §5.7, across attempts rather than blocks. The index leaks nothing, since the acceptance probability does not depend on the secret. The batch is discarded after use: a rejected candidate’s rejection is correlated with the secret, and reusing it would fall outside the theorem. A batch of k fails with probability (1−1/M)k, one percent at 4 candidates for α=48, 11 for α=12 and 33 for α=6; on failure the device samples online. Extraction rewinds until two transcripts use the same index, k+1 transcripts in the worst case instead of two, which costs about log2​k bits of tightness. The merge circuit absorbs the k compressed commitments, four atoms each, and derives c from them.
  • Deferred obligations. The decomposition of z into slices, their commitments, and the range and norm proofs of step 7 need not be the user’s. The aggregator’s first fold decomposes its inputs anyway, and it holds z. So the user hands over z itself, with Cz​=Cy​+c⋅Cs​ computed homomorphically, and the aggregator commits the slices and proves the obligations in its own fold, whose merge circuit checks them as §3.3 describes. The user’s merge circuit checks only the challenge derivation, the commitment identity and the claim fold. Cross-transaction aggregation is not trusted for privacy, and this changes nothing for it: the aggregator received the slices before, which together are z, and it receives z now, which rejection sampling makes independent of s; the obligations it now proves are about z, which it holds, and they guard the decider against a malformed z rather than the transaction against the aggregator, so it checks z’s norm on receipt and refuses a bad one. This is the deferral of open point 7, and it takes nine commitments of N digits and the sum-checks off the device.

What remains online is z=y+cs: a ring product by a sparse ternary challenge, 32 additions per coordinate, and one vector addition, about 227 additions, a tenth of a second on a phone core; the evaluations ui​ of the chosen mask at the claim points; and the transfer of z, about 14 Mbytes at 27 bits per coordinate, 13 Mbytes at α=12 and 12 Mbytes with §5.7’s blocks. The transfer is the cost that does not move, since the information content of z is set by the mask’s width.

5.9 Two matrices: confining the rank to the zero-knowledge layer, and where that stalls

§5.2 charges the masked bound to every step, because every accumulator is committed under the one matrix A whose bound the mask raises, and a smaller matrix for the later folds does not help when it is a prefix of the rows. The other shape is two independent matrices joined by proven equalities, which this section works through to the point where it stalls.

The design. Let A be the accumulation matrix at the ordinary bound, 143 rows over Pasta in §5.3, and A′ a second matrix sized for the masked bound, 349 rows. The user’s own chain runs under A, and so do the aggregator’s merges. Only the handoff touches A′. At the handoff the user commits the last accumulator’s witness s again under A′, Cs′​=A′s, and proves that Cs​ and Cs′​ open to the same short s. The masking fold of §3 then runs under A′. The user hands over z decomposed into its slices, each committed under A and proved equal to its A′ commitment the same way, and the aggregator’s first fold takes the slices as ordinary inputs. The extractor would run in three pieces: the public chain’s, under A at the ordinary bound; the masking fold’s, by the rewinding of §5.2, under A′ at the masked bound; and the user’s chain’s, under A again; the two switches tie the pieces together. That is not the prefix construction §5.2 rules out, since nothing requires the A identities to cover the A′ rows. If it went through, A′ would be used twice per transaction and nowhere else: one more wide commitment, about a third of the masking fold of §5.4, and every step’s commitments would return to the unmasked matrix’s rate.

The switch must be proved. It is not enough that the user computes Cs′​ honestly. The claims (xi​,vi​) folded at the handoff do not bind s. A dishonest user can choose a short s′=s with s′(xi​)=vi​ at the few claim points, which is a system of a few equations in N unknowns, commit s′ under A′, and hand over a masked s′ whose claims pass at the decider. Only the commitment binds the witness, so the switch has to prove that the vector Cs′​ binds is the vector Cs​ binds.

Where it stalls. Accumulation never recomputes a commitment: binding transfers through fold identities that are linear in the commitments, and that is what a change of matrix forfeits, since no linear map takes As to A′s. The direct proof of A′s=Cs′​ for a committed s is a sum-check: the verifier draws r, and the prover shows ⟨A′Tr,s⟩=⟨r,Cs′​⟩. That reduces to an evaluation of s’s multilinear extension, which the accumulator carries as a claim, together with an evaluation of the multilinear extension of A′Tr at the sum-check’s point, which the verifier must compute itself. For a pseudo-random A′ that evaluation is a dense sum over N entries, so the merge circuit that verifies the switch does Θ(N) work, about as much as committing the witness again. Stacking the matrices instead, so that one commitment carries both blocks and the chain checks only the A block, is the prefix construction of §5.2: a cheating prover fills the unchecked block freely. So the switch costs either a linear-size verifier or a matrix with structure that makes A′Tr’s multilinear extension succinct, and Akita’s matrices, expanded from seeds, have no such structure.

The form that would work, and what it costs. An opening at the boundary: fold the user’s witness down through Akita’s own levels to a terminal response short enough that the verifier recomputes its commitment, as the decider does, and have the aggregator’s first merge circuit verify that opening. This seals the handoff the way recursion does (the page’s zero-knowledge paragraph), and it is a decider’s verification inside a step circuit, once per transaction. Its transcript alone is an opening proof of about 85 kbytes to absorb: some 2⋅107 gates with a conventional hash at 14,900 gates per 64 bytes, or about 2⋅105 with Poseidon at 72 gates per atom, before the sum-check arithmetic. What it would save is the masked matrix’s rate on the transaction’s steps and merges. On this section’s Euclidean route that is a factor of 1.7 to 1.9 on their commitments, about a quarter of a second for a 217-gate transaction over Goldilocks at rank 13 on the page, against a masking fold of under half a second. On the page’s ℓ∞​ route (§5.5) it is a factor of 1.0 to 1.33, 14/11 for Kishu, so far less. So with a conventional hash the opening costs several times what it saves per transaction, and with Poseidon the two are close on the Euclidean route and not on the other. System-wide the picture is different, since the masked matrix’s rate is also what every public merge pays, and that is the whole zero-knowledge cost in the page’s merge-prover measure.

So the rank stays with the shared matrix for now. The two-matrix design is worth returning to if either a succinct switch exists for a structured A′, or an in-circuit opening becomes cheap, which the hash policy of the page decides; open point 10.

5.10 A computational hiding padding

The leftover-hash padding of §4.2 is statistical and costs ndlog2​q+2λ uniform bits, several times the statement it hides when the statement is small, as a hardware wallet’s is. A computational padding is a few thousand bits. Append ρ∈{0,1}k to the committed vector, so that Cs​=As+A′ρ with A′ the padding’s columns of the same accumulation matrix. Then Cs​ hides s if A′ρ is pseudorandom: a distinguisher between As+A′ρ and As+u for uniform u is, with As added by the distinguisher itself, a distinguisher between A′ρ and u, with the same advantage and running time. That is the knapsack function of Micciancio and Mol (CRYPTO 2011), fA′​(ρ)=A′ρ over Zqm​ with m the matrix’s scalar rows and k inputs from the uniform binary distribution.

Its pseudorandomness is LWE by a change of coordinates, not by a lossy reduction. A random A′ has full rank m except with probability about q−(k−m), so a row transformation and a column permutation put it in systematic form [B∣I]. Then A′ρ is uniform exactly when Bs′+e is, with (s′,e) the permuted ρ: an LWE instance of secret dimension k−m, m samples, and secret and error both uniform binary. Any distinguisher for one is a distinguisher for the other with the same advantage, up to the linear algebra, which is their theorem. Two heuristics sit underneath, the same two that Akita’s own Module-SIS estimates rest on. The matrix is a module over the ring rather than a uniform Zq​ matrix, and the estimate treats the structured instance as unstructured, since no known attack gains more than small factors from the ring structure. And the error is uniform in {0,1} rather than centred, which is the same instance after subtracting B⋅21​ from the sample, so the cost at σ=21​ is the right one.

The pinned lattice estimator costs every attack on that instance under the ADPS16 quantum model that the page’s Module-SIS instances use (scripts/knapsack-lwe-check.py). The cheapest is the dual hybrid attack, which exploits the binary secret; the primal attacks are about a hundred bits dearer, so a primal estimate alone overstates the margin. At the frontier page’s matrix for the wallet’s statement, 1,024 rows, a padding of 4,800 bits costs the attacker 149 quantum bits, the 147-bit floor’s padding, and one of 4,400 bits 128, so the page takes the least padding on the sweep’s grid, 50 bits where the floors are crossed, that reaches each floor. The padding’s hardness falls with the rows: at this note’s 1,385 Euclidean rows 5,000 bits give 140 bits, and at 2,048 rows they would fall short of the 128-bit floor. Fewer rows mean a larger secret dimension k−m and fewer samples, both of which help the padding. Whether the dual attack’s analysis holds in the regime it is scored in has been disputed (Ducas and Pulles, CRYPTO 2023), so the estimator may credit the attacker with more than the attack delivers; keeping its figure is the conservative choice, as keeping the ADPS16 quantum model is. The statistical padding is still the dearer option by an order of magnitude; the hardware-wallets chapter prices both.

6. Proof hygiene

  • The original Fiat–Shamir-with-aborts analyses had gaps in the treatment of aborted iterations, fixed in 2023 by Devevey–Fallahpour–Passelègue–Stehlé and by Barbosa et al. (both CRYPTO 2023). A proof for the fold should follow a corrected treatment. Two practical consequences: cap the number of attempts, accepting a negligible completeness error, and never publish anything from an aborted attempt.
  • The QROM treatment of Fiat–Shamir with aborts for signatures is Kiltz–Lyubashevsky–Schaffner (EUROCRYPT 2018), the natural starting point here, and separate from Akita’s own QROM proof, which covers the opening protocol.
  • The number of aborts is not in the transcript but is visible to anyone timing the user’s device. Minor for a wallet, but to be noted.
  • The relaxed openings of §5.2 are a soundness matter, not a zero-knowledge one: whatever NARK runs on top of the lattice accumulation must be sound with respect to relaxed openings of its commitments. That is a property of the whole lattice-Ragu design and out of scope here.

7. Open points

  1. Ragu’s fuses now fold two randomizer polynomials as claims of their own and batch a mask, and its rerandomization runs two passes with a public partner (§1.1). Its hiding argument is a per-value accounting with a rank test as evidence, and Ragu’s book and code say the joint distribution is not established. This study does not adopt that argument. Its route is the one-fold statement of §4.3, a single fold of the user’s last accumulator with a uniformly random claim under hiding commitments, with a simulator for everything the aggregator receives: the DL version to be proved first, since its proof is short and fixes the statement, then the lattice version with rejection sampling.
  2. Add a random coefficient to the trace polynomial per evaluation revealed over its lifetime (§4.2). Ragu’s traces and stages now carry three free coefficients each, which its documentation says a parent’s commitment and two evaluations use up; the randomizers do the rest.
  3. Done upstream by the two passes (§1.1): the output shows the first pass’s fresh commitments, not the input’s.
  4. Write the one-fold statement of §4.3 as a theorem and prove it, DL version first, since its proof is shorter and fixes the statement. The DL proof relies on the partner’s own quotient being folded in, which is what makes the map of §1.1 a bijection.
  5. Decide the challenge set and get ∥c∥1​ and the extraction slack from Akita’s planner, then redo §5.3 with real numbers.
  6. Check that the commutation of evaluation with the challenge in step 6 holds for the packing Ragu would use, or choose the packing so that it does.
  7. Settle how the obligations of step 7 are verified, in the user’s merge circuit or deferred with Akita’s fused range and norm checks, and what each costs in gates; §5.8 argues for the deferral.
  8. Decide whether the hiding padding ρ goes into every staged commitment or only into the published ones.
  9. Look for a sign-hiding structure that would make the bimodal variant applicable, saving about 3.6 bits of β and one digit of J.
  10. Revisit the two-matrix design of §5.9 if a succinct proof of a change of commitment matrix appears, for instance from a structured matrix, or if an in-circuit Akita opening becomes cheap enough to seal the handoff.

Hardware wallets and the recovery statement

ZIP 2005’s Recovery Statement needs two authorizations of a recovery spend [ZIP-2005]. One is a RedDSA signature under the randomized key, which FROST makes t-of-n. The other is SoKqsk: a signature of knowledge of the quantum spending key qsk on the transaction’s SigHash, with Hqk(qsk)=qk. The ZIP’s Option A keeps qsk on a hardware wallet, which makes SoKqsk there, and the networked host proves the rest of the statement. This page asks what the wallet can prove and at what cost, and how the signature of knowledge is argued. The figures come from the PCS frontier page, which prices the wallet’s part as applications of its transaction measure. The page was written on 2026-11-21 alongside an analysis of FROST members recovering from a seed phrase, from which it takes the device split.

1. The device split

The model to reason in makes the hardware wallets the only honest parties and treats every networked device as the adversary. A wallet holds the spending key sk, or with FROST its signing share and the common sk, and so qsk. It exports nk and qk and nothing else that is derived from the secret. ak is derived from sk and exported by a single-signer wallet; with FROST it is the output of the distributed key generation. rivk_ext and the incoming and outgoing viewing keys follow from those, so the host can scan, build transactions and produce the main Recovery proof, whose witness is viewing-key material plus the note and its path. ZIP 2005’s other path, use_qsk=false, has the Recovery Statement prove the key derivations from sk itself. It is not considered here, since use_qsk=true is the path whose costs a hardware wallet is meant to optimize.

The wallet signs FROST shares and makes SoKqsk, each after verifying the transaction and asking the user, and the user’s confirmation is the adversary’s choice of message. Two adversary classes share one win condition: a consensus-valid recovery spend on an unapproved SigHash.

  • A pre-quantum adversary corrupts up to t−1 wallets. It is bounded by the unforgeability of re-randomized FROST.
  • A discrete-log-breaking adversary is given every host’s state and every network message, but no wallet. It is bounded by the unforgeability of SoKqsk as a signature scheme with key qk. That bound is 1-of-n, since every wallet holds the same qsk.

Option A is the statement that the second class learns nothing from a wallet but its interface’s outputs.

2. What the wallet can prove

Two shapes of SoKqsk are priced. The wallet can prove its statement as a leaf of the transaction’s own proof system, Kishu on the frontier page. That statement is one BLAKE3 compression, 15,100 committed digits, with the linking commitment of ZIP 2005’s hardware-wallet section left out for now. Or the wallet can sign SigHash with a stateless hash-based signature and leave the verification to the host. The host then proves the verifier inside its own transaction, with the signature and the public key as witnesses, so recovery spends stay unlinkable.

2.1 A Kishu leaf

The handoff is the whole question. The host folds the wallet’s leaf into the transaction’s accumulator, and split accumulation needs the witness of whatever it folds. So the wallet hands over a masked witness: the response z=y+cs of the zero-knowledge note, a Gaussian mask y added to the leaf’s digits s under a challenge c. Rejection sampling makes the accepted z independent of the secret. The mask covers the leaf’s 2rank digits alone, since the wallet hands over no accumulator of its own. The transaction measure charges the user’s handoff the host’s merge that folds the leaf, and a small merge of the handoff’s own: the challenge derivation, the commitment identity, and the claim fold, the decomposition and the range and norm proofs being deferred to the host (the note’s §5.8). For a one-compression leaf the host’s merge is most of the cost. The measure’s 0.0456 s at rank 16 is 83 percent merge and 11 percent fold, and the circuit itself is a few percent.

The wallet need not prove that fold. The note’s §4.2 lists the handoff merge’s witness as simulatable: the hiding commitment, the mask’s commitment, the challenge, the claims and the obligation transcripts. So the host can derive the challenge, prove the fold’s merge and the obligations (the note’s §5.8 deferral), and verify the leaf’s sum-checks in its own merge. The wallet keeps what touches the secret. It commits the leaf with a hiding padding at the masked rank. It proves its constraint and Booleanity sum-checks under Libra-style masking polynomials, 120 committed elements, since the host sees their transcripts. It samples and commits the mask in idle time, and computes the response with the rejection test.

The padding is computational rather than the note’s leftover-hash one. Aρ for ρ of 4,800 uniform bits at the 147-bit floor, the page’s default, or 4,400 at 128, is pseudorandom if knapsack-LWE is hard at the commitment’s rows, which by the Micciancio–Mol duality is LWE of the padding’s bits less the rows, with the rows as samples and binary secret and error at the 64-bit modulus (the note’s §5.10 gives the argument). The lattice estimator puts the cheapest attack on the padding at the matrix’s 1,024 rows at 149 and 128 quantum bits at the two floors’ paddings, under the page’s cost model, a dual hybrid attack on the binary secret; the primal attacks are a hundred bits dearer, so a primal estimate alone would overstate the margin. The padding is the least on the sweep’s grid, 50 bits where the floors are crossed, that reaches the floor, so the hedge of the 147-bit floor applies to it too. At the zero-knowledge note’s 1,385 rows 5,000 bits give 140 bits, and at 2,048 rows they would fall short of the 128-bit floor. The statistical padding would be 66 thousand bits, 4.4 times the statement.

So the wallet commits 27,600 digits. That is 0.256 ms of online work on one M4 core, under a tenth of the handoff fold that the measure charges the user, with 0.389 ms in idle time, and a response of 76 kbytes at 22 bits a coordinate. The device rates are assumptions, scaled from the hash rates that [Wam26]’s hardware-wallet benchmark measured on a Ledger Nano S+: 10 million word multiplications a second for an MCU-class device and 3 million for a secure element. At those rates the computation takes 0.077 and 0.26 s. The transfer of z at that device’s measured 21 kbytes a second over USB takes 3.6 s, or 1.3 s with a pipelined transport. No merge circuit and no accumulator sit on the device, and the witness is 13 kbytes as bits. So a Kishu signature of knowledge is within reach of a high-end hardware wallet on a USB link, and the transfer is the larger part of it.

2.1.1 Why this is not feasible for an animated QR code

An airgapped wallet of the Keystone kind exchanges data by animated QR codes: fountain-coded fragments of a few hundred bytes a frame, at a few frames a second, read by a phone camera from the wallet’s screen. That is a few kilobytes a second at best. The response does not fit that channel, and the reason is not an encoding choice. The accepted z is a Gaussian of width σ on every coordinate of the leaf, about log2​(σ2πe​) bits of information each. It is secret-dependent, so it cannot be regenerated from a seed as the mask can. With no padding and no masking elements the leaf’s own 15,100 coordinates still make 40 kbytes. A succinct Kishu proof of the leaf in place of the response would be about 72 kbytes, whatever the rank from 14 up, since nearly all of it is the opening’s fixed parts, the compression levels and the terminal. A narrower mask saves two or three bits a coordinate at the price of idle-time attempts, and a lighter challenge set a fraction of a bit. The transfer cannot be avoided by moving the fold elsewhere: split accumulation needs the host to hold a witness of the wallet’s accumulator, and that witness is z. So a Kishu-style proof cannot be made small enough for a QR channel. A wallet on such a channel needs the signature of §2.2.

2.2 A hash-based signature

leanSPHINCS, the stateless hash-based signature of post-quantum Ethereum [EIP-8288] [Lit26], fits the QR channel. A signature is 4,276 bytes with [Wam26]’s pruned key of lifetime 230, the configuration priced here, 6,332 with its layered forest key, and 7,740 with Ethereum’s provisional set: a few seconds of scanning. Its signing is hashing alone, measured on a Nano S+ by [Wam26]’s benchmark. The pruned key adds 16,384 grinding digests per signature, 2.8 s with Keccak on that device and 0.50 s with BLAKE2s, and its proved lifetime is 126,900 signatures, one per recovery transaction. The grind is the wallet’s: it is keyed, and the key cannot leave the wallet without revealing which leaves it kept. A full tree can take the host’s help instead. The wallet produces the leaf hashes at key generation, the host builds and stores the tree and supplies the authentication paths, and signing then has no grind.

leanSPHINCS is stateless and deterministic, which matters when every member’s wallet holds the same seed: a stateful scheme’s index would be reused across wallets, and the deterministic randomizer makes the members’ signatures identical.

The host proves the verifier inside its transaction: 298 BLAKE2s compressions or 262 Keccak-f permutations for the pruned key, against 462 and 408 for the layered one and 515 permutations for Ethereum’s. XOR is not free in a digit arithmetization, so in Kishu a Keccak-f permutation is 154,000 committed bits against 21,300 for a BLAKE2s compression. The verifier is therefore 6.39 million digits with BLAKE2s and 40.3 million with Keccak, 6.3 times as many, which is Ethereum’s open hash question seen from the circuit. In a Boolean circuit with XOR free the ratio is 3.3. With zero knowledge Kishu proves the BLAKE2s verifier in 0.297 s on one M4 core at rank 21 and the Keccak one in 1.37 s at rank 22, beside 0.370 s for the recovery circuit itself. Ethereum’s draft fixes Keccak-256 as the scheme’s only primitive; the circuit and the device both argue for BLAKE2s.

What this asks of ZIP 2005 is less than it first seems. Its qk=Hqk(qsk) hashes the secret, and a hash-based signature needs qk to commit to the signature’s public key instead. Deriving that key from the seed inside the Recovery Statement would cost the top layer’s key generation, out of the question. But the derivation is domain-separated. A signature route would define its own derivation of qk from the public key under another context, and the Recovery Statement, which is not yet specified, would accept it as one more arm of its tagged union beside the preimage proof and SoKsk. The arms cannot satisfy each other’s rule, since that would be a collision across two domain-separated hashes. So nothing has to be decided before the scheme is known. The one consequence is that a key derived before the signature route exists is a preimage-route key. A wallet that wants the signature route later needs a new key, which means new addresses and moved funds.

3. The signature of knowledge

A proof of knowledge of a preimage of qk is not enough. It would verify under any transaction, so it could be replayed; the statement has to be signed. The reason goes deeper than replay. The reduction that proves SoKqsk unforgeable, as a signature scheme with key qk, has to answer signing queries without qsk. So it simulates them, and it must then extract a preimage from a forger who has seen simulated proofs. That is simulation extractability, which plain knowledge soundness does not give. A signature of knowledge is by definition a simulation-extractable proof with the message as its label [CL06].

3.1 The folklore technique, and where it is proved

The technique is to bind the message into the Fiat–Shamir transcript from the start. The instance and the message go into the hash before the first challenge, and the chain of challenges binds everything after. Classically this is proved. For sigma protocols it is [FKMV12]. For multi-round sum-check protocols it is recent. [DG23] shows Spartan and Bulletproofs simulation-extractable with no change. [FFKRZ23] and [KPT23] prove it for Fiat–Shamir of a polynomial IOP with a binding commitment in general, under the conditions one expects: the instance hashed first, and a unique-response or state-restoration property of the protocol. The Frozen Heart vulnerabilities of 2022 [TOB22], forgeries against implementations that left the instance out of the hash, are what omitting it costs. The technique is free.

What is missing is the quantum random-oracle model, which the Recovery Protocol needs. Fiat–Shamir of sigma protocols is settled there, by [DFMS19] and [LZ19]. Knowledge soundness of Fiat–Shamir on an IOP is settled with polynomial loss, by [CMS19]. But the multi-round measure-and-reprogram bound [DFM20] loses a factor exponential in the number of rounds, which for thirty sum-check rounds says nothing. And the simulation-extractability proofs above rewind, which the quantum setting does not allow. We know of no simulation-extractability result for a sum-check-based succinct argument in the quantum random-oracle model with usable bounds. In the trust-boundary style of the Ironwood formalization, the signature-of-knowledge property would have to be a named hypothesis.

3.2 A route that is available: the non-injectivity of the hash

A classical argument avoids simulation extractability altogether, and it fits this statement unusually well. Hqk maps 256 bits to 256 bits, so a uniformly random qsk has a second preimage with probability about 1−1/e, 63 percent. The reduction to the collision resistance of Hqk picks qsk itself, answers every signing query with the real prover, and extracts a preimage from the forgery. A zero-knowledge proof is witness indistinguishable [FS90]. So when a second preimage exists, the forger’s view is the same whichever preimage the reduction holds, and the extracted one differs from the reduction’s with probability about a half. Then the reduction holds a collision. The loss is a factor of about 3.2. This is the two-witness form that [KW03] used for tight signature reductions, with the hash’s own non-injectivity standing in for the second key, so the circuit does not change. It needs zero knowledge and knowledge soundness with auxiliary input, the honest signatures on other messages being that input. Both are available in the quantum random-oracle model for the proof systems in play, and the message is still bound into the instance before the first challenge. Nothing in the protocol changes; only the proof does. This is the proof to write for the Kishu route. The hash-based signature route does not raise the question. leanSPHINCS is a signature scheme with its own strong unforgeability proof, 127 classical bits in the random-oracle model [Wam26], and the message enters its digest with the randomizer.
